Moreover, Company B was a Hong Kong company and faced many procedural requirements for inquiries at Mainland government authorities. Third, Company A's performance of the deregistration of the mortgage and its ancillary notification obligation was a prerequisite for Company B to pay the first installment of the second tranche of equity transfer price. When Company A failed to perform the prior notification obligation, Company B had a prior performance defense right for its subsequent payment obligation. Fourth, although Company B was obligated to pay additional taxes according to the contract, there was currently no situation where it had defaulted on tax payments, which had not caused and would not cause any loss to Company A, and did not affect the achievement of the purpose of the contract. Company A had no right to rescind the contract on this basis. (4) Company B and Company C had performed the contract in good faith and paid the equity transfer price in a timely manner as agreed. Company A's assertion that Company B and Company C lacked performance capacity was entirely unfounded. Company B's request for payment in RMB was merely a good faith negotiation during the performance of the contract, and it fully had the capacity to perform. The Transfer Contract should be continued. It requested that Company A's appeal be dismissed.

In response to Company B and Company C's appeal, Company A's defense was consistent with its own appeal arguments and added that Company A, Company D, and Guangzhou Company each maintained separate accounts and ledgers. In actual operations, they did not have the same business, and their managers, financial officers, accountants, etc., were also different. There was no confusion of corporate legal personality, and they should not bear joint and several liability to each other.

In response to Company B and Company C's appeal, Company D and Guangzhou Company's defense was consistent with Company A's defense.

During the second-instance trial of this court, Company A submitted two new pieces of evidence. First, a notarized copy of the "Administrative License Decision" (Yue Si Xu Jue (Fo) Zi [2021] No. 31) issued by the Guangdong Provincial Department of Justice, intending to prove that the two expert institutions participating in the lottery were both controlled by Xiao. The first-instance judgment found that the initiator of Guangdong Tongji Judicial Expertise Center was the Foshan Medical Association and had no subordinate relationship with Xiao, which lacked factual and legal basis. Second, an audit report of Company D for the years 2016 to 2018 issued by Zhongtianyun Haoqin Certified Public Accountants Co., Ltd., intending to prove that Company A had recovered all costs of its investment in Guangzhou Company upon receipt of the first transfer payment of HKD 428,402,985 from Company B and Company C, and therefore should have withheld and paid the tax due before May 17, 2017.

Company B and Company C, in their cross-examination, did not confirm the relevance and purpose of the above two pieces of evidence.

During the second-instance trial, aside from the dispute over whether Company A sent a letter to Company B on June 6, 2017, and the objection to the expert opinion, the parties had no objection to the other facts found by the first-instance judgment. The other facts found by the first-instance judgment are true, and this court confirms them.

It is further found that during the second-instance trial, this court inquired of the parties about the feasibility of conducting an independent inquiry of deregistration of mortgage information and whether Company B had directly gone to the real estate transaction center to inquire. Company A stated that the Measures of Guangzhou Municipality for the Inquiry of Real Estate Registration Materials stipulates that any natural person may inquire about the mortgage registration status of land. Company B stated: (1) In practice, inquiries involving more than five property certificates are considered batch inquiries, and the registration center will strictly review such inquiries out of concern for the potential sale of information. Due to these difficulties, it did not proactively inquire; (2) The payment time for the first installment of the second tranche of equity transfer price under the Transfer Contract was the date of deregistration of the mortgage. If Company A delayed the deregistration, it would have to pay liquidated damages, so Company B had no incentive to inquire on its own.

During the second-instance trial, this court inquired whether Company A had applied for an expert opinion on the handwriting on the June 6, 2017 "Letter." Company A stated that it had applied for such an opinion at first instance, but the first-instance court did not grant it; if Company B and Company C believed the letter was forged, they should have applied for the opinion.

This court holds that this case is a dispute over an equity transfer contract involving foreign and Hong Kong elements. The Transfer Contract stipulates the application of Mainland Chinese law. Pursuant to Article 41 of the Law on the Application of Laws to Foreign-related Civil Relations, which provides that "the parties may choose the law applicable to the contract by agreement," the first-instance judgment correctly applied Mainland Chinese law to resolve this dispute, and this court confirms it. The dispute arose before the implementation of the Civil Code of the People's Republic of China. According to Article 2 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on the Temporal Effect of the Application of the Civil Code of the People's Republic of China, "for civil dispute cases arising from legal facts that occurred before the implementation of the Civil Code, if the laws and judicial interpretations in effect at that time have provisions, those provisions shall apply, except where the application of the provisions of the Civil Code is more conducive to protecting the legitimate rights and interests of civil subjects, maintaining social and economic order, and promoting the core socialist values," this case shall apply the Contract Law and its relevant judicial interpretations.

The issues on appeal are: (1) Whether there was a delay in the payment of the first installment of the second tranche of equity transfer price by Company B; (2) Whether Company A's rescission of the Transfer Contract satisfied the agreed conditions for rescission; (3) If Company A had the right to rescind by agreement, how to determine the legal consequences of rescission and the respective liability for breach of contract of the parties; if it did not have the right to rescind by agreement, whether the Transfer Contract should be continued.

I. On the issue of whether Company B delayed in performing its payment obligation

The Transfer Contract entered into by Company B and Company A concerning the equity transfer and assets of the target company, Company D, reflects the true intention of both parties, does not violate the mandatory provisions of Chinese laws and administrative regulations, is legally valid, and has binding legal force on both parties. Company B paid RMB 100 million to the mainland bank account designated by Company A on April 19, 2017, as agreed, and paid HKD 428,402,985 (equivalent to RMB 380 million) to the Hong Kong bank account designated by Company A on May 10, as agreed. Company A refunded RMB 100 million to Company B on May 9, as agreed, issued a Receipt on May 17 confirming that Company B had duly performed its contractual obligations, and completed the procedures for cancellation of mortgage registration on May 31. Both parties fully performed the agreed obligations under Article 3(2)(1)(a) of the Transfer Contract and were not in breach at that stage. Since the completion of cancellation of mortgage registration is a factual state, the first-instance judgment correctly determined the date of cancellation based on the date recorded on the search report. Company B and Company C's appeal that the date should be determined by the date on which Guangzhou Company received the certificate is inconsistent with the contract's provisions and is not supported by this court.

The dispute over contract performance between the parties arose from the payment of the second installment of the first tranche of equity transfer price. Article 3(2)(1)(b) of the Transfer Contract stipulates: "On the date the cancellation of mortgage registration is completed, Party B shall pay to Party A's designated receiving bank account in Hong Kong an amount in Hong Kong dollars equivalent to RMB 22 million yuan." This court holds that the above clause clearly and unequivocally stipulates the payment amount, method, and time, and its literal meaning is not unclear or ambiguous. However, this court also notes that since the Transfer Contract does not stipulate whether Company A has a notification obligation after completing the cancellation of mortgage registration, the parties have differing views on Company A's notification obligation and whether Company B enjoys a defense to performance due to Company A's breach of the notification obligation. This court addresses these issues separately.

First, whether Company A has a notification obligation. Although the Transfer Contract does not stipulate Company A's notification obligation, under Article 60(2) of the Contract Law, which provides that "the parties shall follow the principle of good faith and perform obligations of notification, assistance, and confidentiality in accordance with the nature and purpose of the contract and trade practices," Company A, as the party who completed the cancellation of mortgage registration, has a statutory obligation to notify Company B on the date of completion. Only in this way can Company B perform its payment obligation on the same day as stipulated in the contract. For Company A, this is also the most convenient and cost-minimizing method of performance, and it is a statutory obligation of cooperation under the principle of good faith.

Second, regarding the nature of the notification obligation and the legal consequences of its breach. The notification obligation is a statutory obligation arising from the principle of good faith, and its nature is an ancillary obligation. Since ancillary obligations are not principal obligations of the contract, a breach of an ancillary obligation does not, in principle, give rise to a defense to performance. Article 66 of the Contract Law provides: "Where the parties owe mutual obligations and there is no order of performance, they shall perform simultaneously. One party has the right to refuse the other party's demand for performance before the other party performs. One party has the right to refuse the other party's corresponding demand for performance if the other party's performance does not comply with the agreement." Article 67 provides: "Where the parties owe mutual obligations and there is an order of performance, the party who is to perform later has the right to refuse the other party's demand for performance if the party who is to perform first fails to perform. The party who is to perform later has the right to refuse the other party's corresponding demand for performance if the party who is to perform first fails to perform in accordance with the agreement." It can be seen that the defense to performance, whether it is the defense of simultaneous performance or the defense of prior performance, has strict prerequisites for application. Where the parties have not explicitly stipulated an ancillary obligation as a principal obligation of the contract, the people's court should not treat the ancillary obligation as a principal obligation or grant the other party a defense of simultaneous performance or even a defense of prior performance for failure to perform the ancillary obligation. Only when a party's breach of an ancillary obligation creates significant difficulty in the other party's performance of the principal obligation, thereby affecting the realization of the contract's purpose, may the other party be granted a defense to performance based on the principle of good faith. This is a special exception and must be strictly limited. The particularity of this case is that the Transfer Contract stipulates that Company B must pay on the date Company A completes the cancellation of mortgage registration. Therefore, the information on when the cancellation is completed is closely related to the payment obligation. If the fact of completion of cancellation is information solely held by Company A and unknown to Company B, then Company B would face significant difficulty in performing its payment obligation, thereby affecting the realization of the contract's purpose. In such a case, it may be determined that Company B enjoys a defense to performance. However, if the above fact is public information that Company B can search for on its own without Company A's cooperation, then the consequence of Company A's delayed notification is, at most, increasing the burden on Company B to conduct its own inquiry, which is insufficient to give rise to Company B's defense to performance.

Third, whether Company B in this case enjoys a defense to performance. The characteristic of ancillary obligations is that the degree of cooperation required between the parties changes as the contractual relationship develops. Therefore, whether a breach of an ancillary obligation affects the realization of the contract's purpose cannot be generalized but must be comprehensively judged in light of the contract performance process and relevant specific circumstances. This court holds that since the Transfer Contract does not stipulate the method of notification, Company A may notify Company B orally or in writing. In this case, Company A has no evidence to prove that it notified Company B on May 31, 2017, and it itself asserts that it first informed Company B on June 6. Therefore, it should be determined that Company A has violated its ancillary obligation. Moreover, based on daily life experience and commercial common sense, it can be presumed that the information that the cancellation of mortgage registration was completed on May 31 was still solely held by Company A, and even if Company B conducted an inquiry, it might not have been able to obtain this information. Therefore, Company A's failure to notify would directly affect Company B's performance of its payment obligation, and Company B enjoyed a defense to performance at this stage.

However, corresponding to Company A's ancillary notification obligation, Company B, as the principal obligor, had a duty of prudent attention and proactive inquiry into the cancellation of mortgage registration as an inherent part of its contractual payment obligation. Particularly as time passed and the parties began to dispute whether Company A had completed the cancellation, Company B should have proactively conducted an inquiry through the Real Estate Trading Center of XX District, Guangzhou, rather than continuously and passively waiting for Company A's notification after sending a letter of inquiry. Article 6(1) of the Measures for Inquiry of Guangzhou Real Estate Registration Information (Sui Guo Fang Zi [2014] No. 209) provides: "Natural persons, legal persons, and other organizations may, by presenting their original identity documents, inquire about the natural condition of real estate and restrictions on rights such as seizure and mortgage." It does not require the inquirer to be a rights holder or interested party. Therefore, the completion of cancellation of mortgage registration is public information available for inquiry. Thus, even if there was a possibility that the cancellation information had not yet been publicly disclosed during the period from May 31 to June 6, 2017, when Company A obtained the titles to the subject real estate, by June 6, when all certificates for the subject real estate were fully processed, the public information on the cancellation was no longer solely held by Company A. Moreover, Company B's representative, Lie, as a professional engaged in real estate investment in the mainland for a long time, faced no legal or factual obstacles in conducting his own inquiry. During the second-instance trial, Company B did not deny that it could inquire but argued that an inquiry involving more than five property certificates constituted a batch inquiry, which the Real Estate Trading Center would strictly scrutinize for suspicion of reselling information, and due to these difficulties, it did not proactively inquire. However, Company B held the Transfer Contract it had signed, which clearly could exclude suspicion of reselling information. This court holds that Company B should have prudently and proactively inquired from June 6, 2017, and its inquiry would not have imposed excessive contractual costs. At that point, Company B no longer enjoyed a defense to performance due to Company A's failure to fulfill the notification obligation. The first-instance judgment, which found that Company B could not learn of the cancellation information without notification and therefore calculated its payment obligation from July 3, when it actually received Company A's written notification, effectively interpreted the contractual provision "payment on the date of completion of cancellation of mortgage registration" as "payment on the date Company A completes cancellation and performs the notification obligation." This interpretation does not conform to the contract and reflects an erroneous understanding of the relationship between ancillary obligations and the defense to performance, constituting errors in fact-finding and application of law. This court hereby corrects this error. In summary, Company B's failure to pay the second installment of the first tranche of equity transfer price on June 6, 2017, constitutes delayed performance of payment and is a material breach.

II. Whether Company A's rescission of the Transfer Contract complies with the contractual conditions for rescission

Pursuant to Article 9(2)(1) of the Transfer Contract, if Company B's overdue payment exceeds 30 days, Company A has the right to rescind the contract. Since Company B no longer enjoyed a defense to performance from June 6, 2017, and remitted the second installment of the first tranche of equity transfer price to Company A on July 20, the overdue payment had exceeded 30 days. In accordance with Article 93(2) of the Contract Law, which provides that "the parties may agree on conditions for one party to rescind the contract. When the conditions for rescission are satisfied, the rescinding party may rescind the contract," Company A has the right to rescind the Transfer Contract. Company A issued a Notice of Rescission of Contract on July 26, 2017, which was served on Company B on the same day, in compliance with Article 96(1) of the Contract Law: "Where a party claims rescission of a contract pursuant to Article 93(2) or Article 94 of this Law, it shall notify the other party. The contract is rescinded when the notice reaches the other party." The Transfer Contract was lawfully rescinded on July 26, 2017. Company A's appeal request for confirmation of the rescission of the Transfer Contract has factual and legal basis and is supported by this court. The first-instance judgment found that Company B's delayed payment did not affect the realization of the contract's purpose and therefore did not constitute a fundamental breach. This contains errors in fact-finding and application of law, and this court hereby corrects it. Given that this court has confirmed the lawful rescission of the Transfer Contract, this court will not review Company A's other grounds for appeal regarding the rescission of the Transfer Contract. This court also will not review or determine the tax-related evidence submitted by Company A in the second instance.

III. Determination of legal consequences after rescission of the Transfer Contract

First, regarding Company A's liability to return the funds held and their interest. Article 97 of the Contract Law provides: "After the rescission of a contract, performance that has not yet been performed shall cease; for performance that has already been rendered, the parties may demand restitution, take other remedial measures, and have the right to claim damages, depending on the circumstances of performance and the nature of the contract." Although Company B and Company C argued for continued performance of the Transfer Contract, they also claimed compensation from Company A for losses resulting from the possession of HKD equivalent to RMB 380 million. This should be regarded as a claim for damages from Company A upon rescission. Therefore, this court addresses the legal consequences after rescission together in its ruling to reduce litigation burden on the parties and facilitate a one-time resolution of the dispute. From the date of rescission, July 26, 2017, Company A was obligated under Article 97 of the Contract Law to make restitution and return the funds paid. Company A's refusal to return the collected equity transfer price lacks contractual and legal basis. It must return HKD 428,402,985 to Company B and Company C, along with interest accrued during the period it held the funds. However, Company B and Company C's appeal request for interest at a monthly rate of 2% on this amount lacks a corresponding contractual basis. Considering that China's foreign currency deposit and lending rate management system underwent major reform from September 21, 2000, allowing financial institutions to set foreign currency lending rates based on international financial market rate changes, capital costs, risk differences, and other factors, it is difficult to determine the Hong Kong dollar lending rate. Therefore, this court, referencing the standard agreed in the Transfer Contract for overdue performance obligations at 0.01% per day, calculates the interest on the base amount of HKD 428,402,985 from July 27, 2017, to the date of performance specified in this judgment. This part of Company B and Company C's appeal request is partially established and is partially supported by this court.

Second, regarding the liability of Company D and Guangzhou Company. Company B and Company C argued that Company A, Company D, and Guangzhou Company should bear joint liability based on the confusion of legal personality among them. However, Article 20(3) of the Company Law provides that the basis for piercing the corporate veil lies in the confusion of corporate personality and the illegal transfer of the company's responsible property based on such confusion, thereby harming the interests of the company's creditors. The parties to the Transfer Contract are Company A. Company D and Guangzhou Company are not shareholders of Company A, and there is no situation where Company A illegally transferred property due to an absolute controlling relationship with Company D or Guangzhou Company. Company B and Company C's appeal request that Company D and Guangzhou Company bear joint liability for Company A's debts lacks legal basis and is not supported by this court.

Third, regarding Company A's contractual liability for breaching the ancillary obligation. Company A failed to perform its ancillary obligation to notify on the day after completing the cancellation of mortgage registration, violating the principle of good faith and having a certain degree of fault. Company B and Company C appealed that Company A should bear liability for breach of contract for overdue handling of equity transfer registration under Article 9 of the Transfer Contract and should pay liquidated damages of RMB 200 million under the provision that either party breaching any term or warranty of the contract shall pay liquidated damages of RMB 200 million. However, as stated above, Company A's obligation was only a statutory ancillary notification obligation, not a contractual or warranted obligation, and Company A was not obligated to handle the equity transfer registration. Therefore, this court does not support this part of Company B and Company C's appeal request. Company A's contractual liability for breaching the ancillary obligation is only reflected in the extension of the due date for the second installment of the first tranche of equity transfer price from May 31, 2017, to June 6, 2017.

Examining the process of both parties' performance, on June 6, 2017, the cooperation between Company B and Company A was still at a harmonious stage. Company B's representative, Lie, during lunch with Company A's representative, Deng A, made a request to change the payment method to RMB. Subsequently, Lie sent WeChat messages with the same content for several days, imploring Deng A. Company B claimed that Deng A did not mention the cancellation of mortgage registration during lunch, but it is inconsistent with daily life experience and commercial common sense that Lie, as a professional engaged in real estate transactions, would so urgently request payment without inquiring about the cancellation status. This is even more inconsistent with the fact that Lie later proactively sent a Letter of Work Contact on June 19 formally requesting to pay RMB 220 million in the mainland. In comparison, Company A's statement that Deng A orally informed Lie on June 6 that the cancellation had been completed is more credible. This court further notes that Company B's position changed starting from the Lawyer's Letter of June 19, in which it claimed that due to Company A's failure to perform the written notification obligation, Company B had no way of knowing the cancellation status of the subject real estate, and that Company A must provide a five-business-day advance notification to allow Company B to prepare funds. However, this content does not conform to the contract and is completely opposite to its earlier proactive attitude towards payment, violating the principle of good faith. Subsequently, on June 23, Lie sent a WeChat message to Deng A suddenly asking, "Have you completed the cancellation for the project?" This court holds that, based on a comprehensive review of the evidence in this case and the series of actions by Company B, it can be corroborated that Company B knew or should have known on June 6 that the cancellation of mortgage registration for the subject real estate had been completed, but encountered difficulties in raising Hong Kong dollars on short notice and therefore hoped to renegotiate the contract. However, regardless of the objective facts of this matter, given that after June 6, Company B could independently inquire about the cancellation status of the subject real estate, whether Company A actually notified Company B on June 6, July 3 (or July 13 as claimed by Company B) is no longer a key factual issue in this case and cannot give rise to Company B's defense to performance. It is unnecessary for this case to conduct a judicial appraisal of Company A's June 6 Letter. This court does not make further evaluation of the judicial appraisal opinion concerning Company A's June 6 Letter, nor does it need to review or determine the evidence related to the judicial appraisal submitted by Company A in the second instance.

Fourth, regarding Company B's liability for damages for breach of contract. Pursuant to Article 97 of the Contract Law, where a contract is rescinded due to a breach, the party entitled to rescind may still claim damages for breach of contract from the breaching party. Article 9.2(1) of the Transfer Contract stipulates that if Company B delays payment of any installment of the transfer price in breach of contract, Company A has the right to demand that Company B perform its payment obligations under the contract within 15 working days, and Company B shall pay liquidated damages at a daily rate of 0.01% of the overdue amount from the due date until the date of full payment. It further stipulates that if Company B's overdue payment exceeds 30 days, Company A has the right to rescind the contract, recover the already transferred equity of the target company, and Company B shall immediately pay liquidated damages of RMB 200 million to Company A. With respect to Company A's appeal request for Company B to pay liquidated damages of RMB 200 million, Company B and Company C did not acknowledge it, implying a claim that the liquidated damages were excessively high and should be reduced. Considering that although the subject matter of the Transfer Contract is the 100% equity and all assets of Company D held by Company A, its value is primarily reflected in the land and above-ground buildings under the name of the Guangzhou company wholly owned by Company D. This land is located in a certain district of Guangzhou, Guangdong Province, and does not suffer depreciation losses due to the rescission of the contract; on the contrary, evidence submitted by Company B shows that the land and above-ground buildings have appreciated. Therefore, upon rescission of the Transfer Contract and restoration to the original state, the value of Company D's equity held by Company A can be correspondingly restored to its original state. On the other hand, pursuant to Article 4 "Equity Transfer and Related Handover Matters" of the Transfer Contract, on the same day all of the first installment of the transfer price is paid in full, Company A shall place all asset certificates, materials, licenses, seals, etc., of Company D and the Guangzhou company under joint management with Company B or its designee, and shall transfer 51% of Company D's equity to Company B or its designee within three working days. Article 9 "Liability for Breach of Contract", subparagraph 2(1), provides that the return of the already transferred equity and the payment of liquidated damages of RMB 200 million together constitute liability for restoration to the original state and compensation for losses. Thus, the function of the RMB 200 million liquidated damages is to compensate for losses incurred at the stage of contract performance where the equity has already been transferred. However, in this case, the rescission of the Transfer Contract occurred at a performance stage before the second sub-installment of the first installment was fully paid, and the equity held by Company A had not yet been transferred. Company A also failed to adequately prove the losses caused by the rescission of the Transfer Contract. Therefore, Company A's appeal request for RMB 200 million in liquidated damages lacks sufficient factual and legal basis and is not supported by this Court. Nevertheless, Company A is entitled, pursuant to Article 9.2(1) of the Transfer Contract, to claim from Company B liquidated damages for the overdue payment of the second sub-installment of the first installment of the equity transfer price, calculated at a daily rate of 0.01% on the principal amount of HKD 254,570,700 from June 6, 2017 (the due date for the second sub-installment of the first installment of equity transfer price) to July 20, 2017 (the date Company B actually paid but the payment was returned). Company C, as the transferee designated by Company B under the Transfer Contract, not only paid the equity transfer price during performance but also jointly sent letters with Company B to assert rights against Company A. Therefore, Company C is a joint transferee with Company B and shall bear joint and several liability for discharge together with Company B.

Finally, it must be pointed out that this dispute arose because both parties lacked a correct legal understanding of the principle of good faith and the ancillary duty of notification. Had there been proper communication at the initial signs of disagreement, the expansion of the dispute could have been completely avoided. However, due to poor communication between the parties after June 19, 2017, and the overly aggressive wording in the exchanged Lawyer's Letters and Work Contact Letters, trust fell to freezing point, ultimately leading to the breakdown of the cooperative relationship. This was certainly not the original intention of the parties' business cooperation. It is hoped that this case can serve as a basis for the parties to rebuild mutual trust on a rational foundation and avoid becoming mired in years of litigation.

In summary, the first-instance judgment contained errors in both factual findings and the application of law and should be corrected. The appeal grounds of Company A, Company B, and Company C are partially meritorious, and this Court partially upholds them. Pursuant to Article 8, Article 60, Article 93(2), Article 96, and Article 97 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China, Article 2 of the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on the Temporal Effect of the Application of the Civil Code of the People's Republic of China, and Article 177(1)(2) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, this Court hereby renders judgment as follows:

1. The civil judgment (2017) Yuemin Chu No. 61 of the Guangdong High People's Court is set aside;

2. It is confirmed that the Equity and Asset Transfer Contract signed between Company A and Company B on April 18, 2017, was rescinded on July 26, 2017;

3. Company A shall, within ten days after this judgment takes effect, return to Company B and Company C HKD 428,402,985 and the interest losses during the period of possession (calculated at a daily rate of 0.01% on the principal amount of HKD 428,402,985 from July 27, 2017, to the date of satisfaction of the payment as determined herein);

4. Company B and Company C shall, within ten days after this judgment takes effect, pay to Company A liquidated damages for overdue payment (calculated at a daily rate of 0.01% on the principal amount of HKD 254,570,700 from June 6, 2017, to July 20, 2017);

5. All other counterclaims of Company A are dismissed;

6. All other claims of Company B and Company C are dismissed.

If any monetary payment obligation is not performed within the period specified in this judgment, the defaulting party shall, in accordance with Article 260 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, pay double the interest on the debt for the period of delayed performance.

For first-instance court fees, the fee for the principal claim is RMB 6,541,800 and the preservation fee is RMB 10,000, totaling RMB 6,551,800. Company B and Company C shall bear RMB 5 million, and Company A shall bear RMB 1,551,800. The fee for the counterclaim is RMB 3,270,900. Company A shall bear RMB 2,270,900, and Company B and Company C shall bear RMB 1 million. For second-instance court fees of RMB 9,342,266.77, Company B and Company C shall bear RMB 6 million, and Company A shall bear RMB 3,342,266.77.

This judgment is final.
